beliefs.practice: Read the cluster connection string from an environment variable (e.g., DOCUMENTDB_URI) at runtime and never commit the URI, credentials or any secrets into source control; provide a .env.example with a placeholder instead.

Connect with the MongoDB driver/Mongoose using TLS/SSL (set tls=true or tls=true&tlsAllowInvalidCertificates=false in the connection string) and verify server certificates (rejectUnauthorized true) to ensure encrypted transport.
Use a least-privilege database user for the app (a MongoDB user with only the required roles on the sample_retail_20 database) instead of the cluster admin/root credentials.
Open and reuse a pooled MongoDB connection (configure maxPoolSize in the connection options and use Mongoose's single connection for the app) instead of creating a new connection per request.
Set sensible socket and operation timeouts (e.g., socketTimeoutMS and serverSelectionTimeoutMS) and configure maxPoolSize to protect the client from hanging or exhausting connections under load.

Model GeoJSON Points exactly as { type: 'Point', coordinates: [lng, lat] } in the Mongoose schema, validate the type enum and coordinate array length, and store a single location field per store for 2dsphere queries.

Create a 2dsphere index on the GeoJSON location field with createIndex({ location: '2dsphere' }) (do this before running geo queries), and verify the index exists on the sample_retail_20.stores collection.

Create required indexes (2dsphere and others) as part of deployment/ops (index creation script or DB migration) rather than relying solely on Mongoose autoIndex in production; if using Mongoose autoIndex, enable it only in development.

When performing geospatial ranking use an aggregation with a $geoNear stage as the first stage, supplying near: { type: 'Point', coordinates: [...] }, distanceField, and maxDistance (meters) to filter by radius and sort by distance.

Ensure $geoNear uses GeoJSON coordinates (lng, lat) and include spherical: true when required so distances are computed on a sphere (include distanceMultiplier if you want kilometers instead of meters).
Limit fields returned by the /nearby endpoint (project only the fields the client needs—location, distance, hours, stock) to reduce network payload and RU/IO consumption.
Use pagination (limit + skip or use range-based cursors) for large result sets and avoid unbounded queries from the /nearby endpoint so you don't exceed resource limits or return massive arrays.
Implement retry with exponential backoff for transient errors and rate-limited responses (HTTP 429) and honor Retry-After header returned by the service to avoid immediate repeated throttling.

Handle common MongoDB error codes returned by the server (connection timeout, network error, cursor timeout, 50x server errors) and fail gracefully in the API with appropriate HTTP status codes and messages.
Seed scripts should be idempotent: create collections and indexes only if missing, upsert documents or check existence before inserting, and log actions so they can be safely re-run during CI or ops.

Monitor query performance and index usage (explain plans for the $geoNear aggregation) and ensure the geo query is using the 2dsphere index; if the explain shows COLLSCAN, fix the index/field mapping.

When using Mongoose, disable autoIndex in production (set autoIndex: false in the connection options) and perform index builds as part of controlled deployment steps because index builds can be resource-intensive.
Validate and sanitize lat/lon inputs on the /nearby endpoint (ensure numeric ranges: lat between -90 and 90, lon between -180 and 180) and enforce a maximum radius to prevent abusive queries.

If the cluster supports vector search, do not enable or create vector indexes on collections that don't need them (vector indexes increase storage and compute); keep vector and geo workloads separated into different collections where possible.

Provision adequate cluster resources for the expected index and query workload (choose an instance/tier with enough memory and IO for 2dsphere index operations) and scale up if you see index builds or queries thrashing the disk.
Avoid long-running blocking index builds at peak time—create indexes during maintenance windows or use the provider’s recommended online/background index build option to avoid downtime.
Use meaningful index names and include them in deployment manifests or migrations so operators can reconcile indexes created by the app vs indexes created by ops tooling when troubleshooting.
Log the aggregation pipeline and explain() output in non-sensitive logs when debugging query performance, but avoid logging full connection strings or credential data.
